---
title: "Random seeds"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true

---

A pseudorandom generator produces a deterministic sequence from an initial state. A [**random seed**](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/Random.html) records that state, allowing a stochastic computation to be reproduced exactly. Reproducing a sequence preserves the same algorithmic draws from the target [PMF](probability-mass-functions.qmd); it does not collect new linguistic observations.

The integers used below are arbitrary labels for generator states. Their
magnitudes have no probabilistic meaning. A generator state determines where
the next call begins in a deterministic pseudorandom stream; it does not make
the simulated observations statistically independent of the model that
generated them.

We rebuild the Turkish lemma sampler, repeat it under matching and different seeds, and then separate computational reproducibility from replication with newly collected linguistic data.

## Repeating the Turkish lemma sampler

This page reloads the BOUN interrogative table and reconstructs the [inverse-transform sampler](inverse-transform-sampling.qmd). The sample size and seeds below are computational settings; the target probabilities still come from the corpus.

```{r}
#| label: seed-ud-questions
library(ggplot2)

questions <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
counts <- as.data.frame(table(questions$lemma), responseName = "count")
names(counts)[1] <- "lemma"
counts$probability <- counts$count / sum(counts$count)
cutpoints <- cumsum(counts$probability)

inverse_sample <- function(n, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  u <- runif(n)
  index <- findInterval(u, c(0, cutpoints), rightmost.closed = TRUE)
  index[index > nrow(counts)] <- nrow(counts)
  counts$lemma[index]
}

n_draws <- 250L
seed_a <- 20261018L
seed_b <- 20261019L
draw_a1 <- inverse_sample(n_draws, seed_a)
draw_a2 <- inverse_sample(n_draws, seed_a)
draw_b <- inverse_sample(n_draws, seed_b)

same_seed_identical <- identical(draw_a1, draw_a2)
different_seed_identical <- identical(draw_a1, draw_b)
target_ne <- counts$probability[counts$lemma == "ne"]

paths <- rbind(
  data.frame(draw = seq_len(n_draws),
             cumulative_ne = cumsum(draw_a1 == "ne") / seq_len(n_draws),
             sequence = "seed A"),
  data.frame(draw = seq_len(n_draws),
             cumulative_ne = cumsum(draw_b == "ne") / seq_len(n_draws),
             sequence = "seed B")
)

stopifnot(
  same_seed_identical,
  !different_seed_identical,
  all(paths$cumulative_ne >= 0 & paths$cumulative_ne <= 1)
)

data.frame(
  comparison = c("same seed", "different seeds"),
  identical_sequence = c(same_seed_identical, different_seed_identical)
)
```

Calling `set.seed()` restores the generator state. The same sampler then consumes the same uniform sequence and returns the same lemma sequence. The second seed changes the Monte Carlo realization but not the target PMF.

Setting the seed *inside* a reusable function has a cost: every call with the
default seed would return the same draws, even when a caller expects fresh
Monte Carlo replicates. A more composable design sets the seed once in the
analysis script and lets the function consume the current stream, or accepts a
seed only when exact per-call reproduction is explicitly wanted.

```{r}
#| label: plot-seed-ud-questions
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative simulated proportion of ne under two seeds. The horizontal line is the empirical target probability."
ggplot(paths, aes(draw, cumulative_ne, color = sequence)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = target_ne, color = "grey35", linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.75) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("seed A" = "#8B1A1A", "seed B" = "grey55")) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  labs(x = "Simulated draw", y = "Cumulative proportion of ne", color = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Both paths fluctuate because each is finite. A seed makes those fluctuations inspectable and debuggable; choosing a different seed is not a robustness analysis by itself. Robustness requires examining the distribution of results across many [independently generated](../foundations/independence.qmd) sequences—sequences whose simulated draws do not change one another's modeled probabilities—or using an exact calculation when one is available.

This fluctuation is [**Monte Carlo error**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html), the gap between a finite simulation
summary and its target under the simulation model. It is distinct from
sampling uncertainty in the corpus and from model misspecification. The [later
Monte Carlo treatment](../statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd#two-uncertainties)
separates these uncertainties formally.

## Check your understanding

1. Confirm that `draw_a1` and `draw_a2` agree element by element.
2. Move `set.seed()` outside the function and explain how the behavior changes.
3. Repeat the final proportion across many seeds and plot its distribution.
4. Why does setting a seed not address sentence-level dependence in the corpus?
5. Why can resetting one fixed seed inside every bootstrap replicate invalidate
   the intended comparison across replicates?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. `identical(draw_a1, draw_a2)` is `TRUE`, so the two same-seed draws agree element by element. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. With `set.seed()` outside the function, successive calls consume later parts of the random stream and differ, though rerunning the whole seeded sequence remains reproducible. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Across seeds 1–1,000 with 250 draws each, the *ne* proportion has mean 0.878912, standard deviation 0.021040, and range 0.804–0.940 around the empirical target 0.880240. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. A seed controls computational reproducibility but does not change the fact that corpus tokens can share sentences, registers, or other sampling units. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Every replicate would reuse the same pseudorandom choices instead of
   advancing to a new resample, so the apparent collection of replicates could
   contain duplicates by construction.

</details>

A seed is an arbitrary label for a computational state. Reproducing that state
does not establish statistical independence, and Monte Carlo error is not the
same as corpus sampling uncertainty. The [joint-distribution
page](joint-probability.qmd) now turns from simulation to paired measurements in
the English dative data.
